planting.note: Divide the creeping rhizome or root leaf cuttings in spring, growing as a houseplant or shaded container plant that can summer outdoors in zone 9 and warmer; it cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Begonia manicata is a Mexican rhizomatous species named for the thin fringe of reddish hairs that rings the leaf stalks and stipules like a cuff. Glossy, rounded, plain deep-green leaves sit atop a thick, creeping surface rhizome, while the widely grown Aureomaculata form carries irregular gold-yellow blotches across the same leaf shape. Tall, airy sprays of small, pale pink flowers rise well above the foliage in late winter and early spring, a welcome bonus on a plant grown chiefly for its leaves. Keep the rhizome sitting on top of the mix rather than buried, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings to avoid crown rot.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

planting.note: Root two-node cane cuttings in moist perlite or water, planting out as a shrubby container specimen after frost danger passes; grow outdoors year-round only in zone 10 and warmer.

directions: Begonia coccinea is the true Brazilian cane-type species behind many of the familiar angel-wing hybrids, forming tall, jointed, bamboo-like canes clothed in smooth, pointed, olive-green leaves. Hanging clusters of waxy, coral-scarlet flowers appear repeatedly through the warm months, held on long stalks well clear of the foliage. Left unpinched it grows as a narrow, upright shrub that can tower over most other begonias, so pinching young canes early encourages a fuller, more branched silhouette. Give it bright, filtered light rather than deep shade and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings to keep the thick canes from rotting at the base.

planting.note: Divide the thick surface rhizome or root a leaf-petiole cutting in spring; grow as a houseplant everywhere but zone 10-11, where it can summer outdoors in bright shade.

directions: Begonia heracleifolia earns its common name from deeply cut, star-shaped leaves that echo the foliage of cow parsnip, held on long, slightly hairy petioles rising from a thick, creeping rhizome. Mature leaves can take on a bronzy cast along the lobes and veins, and a dense covering of fine hairs gives the whole plant a soft, matte texture quite different from the glossy sheen of rex begonias. Clusters of pale pink to white flowers rise on tall, wiry stems well above the foliage mound in winter and early spring. It tolerates lower light and drier air better than most rhizomatous begonias, making it a forgiving choice for a shaded windowsill or terrarium edge.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water and plant out as a container shrub after frost danger passes; keep as a houseplant outside of zone 10-12.

directions: Begonia sanguinea is a Brazilian cane-type species prized for the striking contrast between its thick, glossy, deep-green leaf surfaces and the solid blood-red undersides for which it is named. The fleshy, almost succulent leaves sit on sturdy jointed stems, and small greenish-white flowers appear in loose clusters but are secondary to the dramatic two-toned foliage. Grow it in bright, indirect light rather than deep shade to keep the stems from stretching, and let the mix dry slightly between waterings since the thick leaves and stems store some moisture.
